hint: Hover or tap a part of either option.

parts.title: Option 1 · SoundHub
parts.body: SoundHub's backend checks the user's access and builds the explicit list of recordings. It installs no ROBIN code.

parts.title: Option 1 · ROBIN as a service
parts.body: Our team runs ROBIN's API server, run manager, controller and database as a separate service that other programs could share.

parts.title: Option 1 · POST /v1/runs
parts.body: SoundHub's backend calls ROBIN's API over HTTP with the work request as JSON. Open question: how the API trusts SoundHub's backend and names the user.

parts.title: Option 1 · Detections via api-dock
parts.body: api-dock, run by our team, reads ROBIN's published views and serves detections back to SoundHub.

parts.title: Option 1 · AWS
parts.body: The controller launches SageMaker jobs that read audio from S3. Jobs still need their own access to SoundHub's audio.

parts.title: Option 1 · Trade-offs
parts.body: Clean separation and independent releases, at the cost of one more service and one more database for our team to run.

parts.title: Option 2 · SoundHub's web app and backend
parts.body: The backend checks its own users and calls ROBIN directly. There is no API to secure.

parts.title: Option 2 · ROBIN as a library
parts.body: SoundHub installs ROBIN unchanged. The run manager is called in the same process, and the controller runs as a background worker.

parts.title: Option 2 · One PostgreSQL
parts.body: ROBIN's tables live in their own schema inside SoundHub's database, so there is only one database to run.

parts.title: Option 2 · AWS
parts.body: The controller launches SageMaker jobs with SoundHub's own AWS role.

parts.title: Option 2 · Trade-offs
parts.body: One deployment and no API to secure, but SoundHub takes on ROBIN's dependencies and migrations, and its releases are tied to ROBIN's.
